utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution would like to raise a preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. And thank you. The preliminary matter I'd like to raise relates to Rule 90(E). A number of the upcoming witnesses - in fact, the witness that's presently giving evidence - the Karadzic Chamber took the view that they needed to be given the 90(E) warning. I'm not sure whether it's appropriate for the Prosecution to be requesting that. We don't really know all that much about these witnesses. It seems that perhaps the Defence in their dealings with the witnesses and their conversations with the witnesses may be in a better position to know whether that would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: (redacted) At the very least, we think maybe we are obliged to advise the Chamber when a witness has received that warning in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, the Chamber will in due course pay appropriate attention to the matter you have just raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then is the Defence ready to continue its examination-in-chief of the witness? Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Skrba. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration you gave yesterday, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, is still binding upon you. That goes perhaps even without saying, but I just remind you. Mr. Stojanovic will now continue his examination-in-chief. Please do so, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Skrba.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have document D465 in e-court. It was marked for identification yesterday when we adjourned. Thank you. I would like to ask the usher to help the witness use the blue pen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, now I'd like to ask you the following: If you remember yesterday, we marked the location of the command of the mixed artillery battalion and the position of the 120-millimetre mortar company. Could you mark on this map for the Court the area of the left flank of the area that you covered with your units?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The left flank is the Zeljeznica river-bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to use that blue marker that you have to mark that particular position.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Down here in this corner? I cannot. There is no image.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase. Was Ilidza the area that your mixed artillery battalion covered?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilidza fell under a different group, the Ilidza Brigade. They had their own responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I'm going to ask you, precisely for that reason, the area of Butmir, did it fall under the command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, from the positions that you covered, your unit, the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, did it come under artillery fire that came from the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, constantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What were the most frequent positions where you suffered most of that fire?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mobile mortars, Ciglana, the tunnel, Debelo Brdo, Zuc, vis-à-vis our positions, Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From the area of Ciglana, did you identify the weapons that were used to target your positions by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had heavy weapons all the time. They got it out of the tunnel and they fired at us at will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could we seek more specific answers. "They had heavy weapons all the time." What heavy weapons are you referring to and do you know the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do it exactly that way in the right order, by your leave, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As for Ciglana, the area that we talked, did you identify the heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A tank, T-100 and T-55, they were the ones that were opening direct fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From the area of Bjelave, can you tell the Court what kind of weaponry was used by the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area they used 120-millimetre mobile mortars mounted on a vehicle. It depended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From the area of Trebevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I gave a suggestion, also the number. Could you ask for the number of 120-millimetre mobile mortars which were available to the opposing armed forces? I'm now focusing on Bjelave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our intelligence would have that exact information. I was just observing the points from where the fire came and I tried to neutralise that fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any intelligence as to how many 120-millimetre mortars they had in Bjelave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They always had at least two to four at those firing positions from where they opened fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, the question also had to do with the area of Trebevic. Did you identify the weapons that were used?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 82-millimetre mortars for the most part, and also there were two 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell the Court about the hill of Zuc. Did you identify the weapons that were used to target your positions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a tank there that was on the move all the time, and then they used this M-55 tank to fire at us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we still do not have an estimate of the numbers for the 82-millimetre mortars on Trebevic. How many 82-millimetre mortars were there on Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usually platoons were established with three mortars. Now, it depends on whether there was a complete battery there with six or a platoon with three. It depended on that moment, at that moment, whether they were carrying out operations in different directions and whether they had them located in different areas so that they would pretend to carry out false attacks in order to deceive the other side. But it depended --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak slower. And we did not catch the last sentence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, the interpreters ask whether you could speak a bit slower. They have difficulties in following the speed of your speech. Second, would you please repeat the last part of your answer. I'll read what is still on the record and then could you please repeat what you said after that. It is recorded that you said that: "They had them located in different areas so that they would pretend to carry out false attacks in order to deceive the other side. But it depended ..." And then you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It depended on what the main thrust of their attack would be, and then, along that line, they would concentrate a larger number of mortars that they had available; whereas on the auxiliary axes of attack, there would usually be three or four weapons that would usually have ammunition. However, as far as the main line of attack was concerned, there would always be three times more weapons, ammunition, et cetera, depending on what they wanted to target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a long answer, but, Mr. Stojanovic, to be honest, I can't say that I now have a clear idea on how many mortars they had available. But if you want to further clarify, please do so. If not, just for you to know that the numbers are not that clear to me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just put one more question in this regard and then I think I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The number of mortars at these locations during the war, was it permanent throughout or would it happen that depending on war developments, the intensity of fighting, et cetera, that these mortars would move?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was always a permanent number, a certain permanent number. A platoon would have three pieces but they would supplement it with more pieces if that is where the main thrust of their attack was. Then they would increase the number to six, twelve mortars, depending on the amount of ammunition they had and what their ultimate objective was in terms of that particular direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to ask you about an area, a part of Sarajevo, Velesici [Realtime transcript read in error "Bjelisici"]. In that area, in that part of the city of Sarajevo, did they have weapons, artillery pieces that they used against you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said, below Hum, in Velesici, they had a tank, a T-55 that they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did they have the possibility of concealing that tank from the artillery positions of your unit?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the weaponry was in depth and outside the centre of the zone, the civilian population, they had these shelters, they concealed this, and also they had a large area. They could move left or right a kilometre or two, so they changed the location from which they were firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'll conclude with this question: As for the external ring, as we called it, the encirclement behind your back from Igman and the other heights behind you, were you under artillery fire coming from there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had the same number of fatalities on the external ring just like on the internal ring re the artillery men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'll conclude by asking whether you established from which positions on the external ring the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina targeted your positions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main positions were on Mount Igman, outside Sarajevo, Hrasnica, and that is primarily where they fired from. Until Lukavac 93 was over, they fired from Trnovo and Rogoj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Aware of the fact that the area of Butmir was not within your area of responsibility, I'd like to ask: Did you have the possibility to observe whether from the agricultural complex or institute those assets were used against your positions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From our observations points, whenever they launched attacks we would see the fire, the explosions of mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, considering that we did not use D465 and we didn't mark it anymore, and this document has already been MFI'd, I would now like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and there is no need to replace it in the absence of any further markings. Madam Registrar, D465 is now admitted into evidence. Before we take -- I have one or two additional questions for you, Mr. Skrba. You told us about the tank in Velesici, although in the question it is called Bjelisici, but you talked about the tank which was concealed and moved for perhaps a kilometre. How were you coping with that problem? If it was concealed, you couldn't see it. Let me just see, do you have problems in -- you can hear my question? My question was if they were concealing that tank in that area, so you couldn't see it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I completely understand the question, but the tank, after firing three or five shells, would go back into shelter, would hide in a trench. And it was a wooded area, it was easy to hide it. But you could see by the smoke and the reaction of the weapon, you could see the flash of the explosion. But they never left it in one place for a long time. Just as long as it took to fire a couple of shells and then it would move back. And it wasn't in one fixed place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that you said it was a wooded area. Does this mean that it was not a -- no people were living there or was there -- was the area sparsely populated? Could you tell us a bit more about ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's the area of Pofalici, towards Hum, it was 80 per cent Serb population. But after the actions of the ABH, the Serb population was expelled from that neighbourhood, Sikirasi and Hum, the ABH army occupied these elevations and turned it into their own firing positions. And they had complete control over that area because there were no longer any Serbs there. And they used all the features there. They used it as accommodation for troops and emplacements for tanks and other assets. They would build a makeshift roof or tent for the tank and you would never be sure whether it's there or not. After 1993 and 1994, they cut most of the woods so it was easier to notice the tank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, is there any documentary evidence which would support what you just told us, to your knowledge? Any written orders or?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know it so well. If we take the dates of their celebrations when they had major victories, they would show it on film and on television, and, of course, everybody could see it and it's well documented because they celebrated these major breakthroughs and victories after which they managed to control the territory they wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean documentary evidence from within the Army of the Republika Srpska, whether this was reported: "We fired at the tank which was then in hiding again," or whatever. Is there any reporting or any orders received to especially focus on those tanks? Is there any documentary evidence from within your armed forces about what you just told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any orders to fire to the area of Pofalici without a tank having been detected or having been discussed? Just fire at Pofalici, for example, are you aware of any possible order to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't receive any such orders and I did not hear such orders through our communications because it was under a completely different military unit. That area was under the Vogosca Brigade and we were facing them. We were on the opposite side to the south-east from Pofalici and Hum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I understood your evidence to tell us what -- let me just see. So if you saw that tank firing, et cetera, you didn't respond in any way. You didn't return fire from your positions. It's just -- you just observed it and that's it? Because you were fired at, if I do understand you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. But when we noticed the tank, in order to return fire we had to prepare. We would return fire with one or two shells, and after that, the tank would go back to its shelter. We had observation points on Mount Trebevic and we could observe it, but we could actually react only when it opened fire against our firing positions. But physically, it was in the territory covered by the Vogosca Brigade which was, in its turn, unable to see all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do not understand your reference to the Vogosca Brigade, because you tell us: "We were fired at by a tank, we returned fire." Now, I do understand that Pofalici is closer to the area of responsibility of the Vogosca Brigade, but they couldn't do anything. They didn't see anything. They didn't -- I don't know whether they were fired at from that area as well. It's a bit unclear why you are referring to the Vogosca Brigade rather than to your own artillery.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry. Vogosca Brigade was, like, behind your back and the tank was front of them, and they couldn't see this tank; whereas we were fired at directly because they were on higher ground and targeted us directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that point. But when I asked you about orders, you said you never did receive any such orders such as fire at Pofalici, and you said you did not hear such order through your communications because it was under a completely different military unit. That area was under the Vogosca Brigade, but nevertheless, you engaged targets in that area from your positions; whereas the Vogosca Brigade apparently was not in a position to see anything and therefore would also not engage any targets in that area, or would they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not fire because they couldn't observe it, they couldn't see the point from which fire was opened. Only we could see it from Trebevic and Vrace. And we would do so when we saw two or three shells fired. But, of course, we asked approval from our superior command whether we could return fire and then we would fire two or three projectiles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. We will deal with another matter before we start your cross-examination. So therefore most likely the break will be a bit longer than usual, more than 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after the break, Mr. Skrba, and I'll invite the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We take a bit of an early break and we will resume at 20 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Shin, it will be you who will cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And your time estimate was two hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe our time estimate was three and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that remained three and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, as I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, the other -- one of the other witnesses, I think, was reduced to two hours but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I believe I saw that recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps that's wishful thinking. Please be seated, Mr. Skrba. Mr. Skrba, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Shin. You'll find Mr. Shin to your right. Mr. Shin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Skrba.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'd like to start with some questions about the organisation of the mixed artillery battalion, the MAD, and your position in the MAD. And just to be clear, the MAD is immediately subordinate to a brigade, like an infantry battalion. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have difficulties in hearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not been receiving interpretation into Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's check whether you're on the right channel. Okay. Let's start again. Do you now hear me in a language you understand? That's right, you're not hearing me but you're hearing the interpreter. Mr. Shin, could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- give it another try.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, I will start again with my question since I believe you did not hear the translation. What I was saying was that I would like to start with some questions about the organisation of the mixed artillery battalion and your position in that unit. And just so that -- just to begin with, to be clear, the mixed artillery division, the MAD, that's immediately subordinate to the brigade, like an infantry battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit's name was mixed artillery division, and the name "artillery division" was given to it because all the artillery pieces were in my unit under my command. I only supported infantry in defence and attacks. The only infantry weapons we had were in the hands of the soldier, and I told you what we had in terms of artillery pieces. I can repeat it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, perhaps my question wasn't clear. We'll take this step by step and we'll address some of the issues you're anticipating here. But just perhaps for a point of clarity at this point, you referred to the mixed artillery division. It's at the same level as an infantry battalion. Would that be correct? And I'm simply talking here in terms of what the immediate superior command was to you. That would be the brigade command, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: However -- just a moment. However, a mixed artillery division has its power in the artillery pieces that it has, whereas infantry or a battalion has a different force of firing power. We are talking about two different paths of a military; artillery on the one hand and infantry on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That's correct and that's probably apparent in the title, that one is an artillery unit and the other is an infantry unit. Now, how many men were in the MAD?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since its members were locals and for each of the actions that were undertaken at firing positions of those units, and batteries are lower than battalions, and their specialties, their topographies, commanders, telephone operators, logistics units that supported their own unit and so on and so forth. And they differed in terms of the types of weapons they had, i.e., its calibre. Therefore we had --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, if -- could we agree -- if you could just listen carefully to my question. There may be an opportunity to add additional information, but please listen to my specific question and if you could answer the question, we will be able to get along a little more smoothly here. My question to you was simply how many men were in the MAD.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had only 35 to 40 per cent of the men that I was supposed to have according to my formation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, no one asked you whether you were understaffed or overstaffed. Mr. Shin just asked you how many men was that, 20, 100? Just give a number and try to focus on the question. How many men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 350 men all together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Carefully listen to the next question and try to answer it directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, my next question is: How were these 350 men organised? And just to focus this question a little bit, I will remind you that you have spoken about both platoons and batteries. Could you explain if that -- in those types of units, is that how those 350 men were organised, and if so, how many batteries, how many platoons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that I had six batteries. Each of the batteries had either two or four firing platoons, and platoons were divided into squads. There was a command squad which consisted of scouts or reconnaissance men, and there was a topographist and also a communications staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you referred to the command squad of a platoon. What rank typically would a platoon -- I'm sorry, would the commander of a command squad have?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the availability, but it should have been a junior officer, a warrant officer. It depended on what we had, whether we had trained personnel or whether we had to train somebody we had and was not properly trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll get to some of those issues, but to help us with one other bit of terminology here. The term "battery," would it be correct that in general the term "battery" is used to comprise -- sorry, the term "battery" is used to describe a unit that has four to six guns or barrels?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A battery would be a basic military formation. Such a battery, if it was full and complete, it would have about 72 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was how many guns, four to six.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that if it was fully staffed, it would have 72 men who would man artillery pieces and they would also be assigned to accompanying squads, the command squad, and all the other accompanying units that were logistics for those men, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are talking about men. Mr. Shin was asking about the number of barrels in such a battery. He suggested four to six. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D30 batteries, 120-millimetres. There were three batteries, each had four barrels and four squads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And maybe we'll try this: To have four barrels in a D30 battery, would that be a typical number for a D30 battery?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In formation terms, if we had enough men that battery should have had six barrels and six squads, each of them having seven men that would serve those barrels. And there would also be the so-called services, communications, reconnaissance squad, irrespective of the fact whether there were four barrels or six barrels because they would still have to do -- they would still have to prepare things. For one barrel or for six barrels it would be the same. We had three D3 batteries, three groups, and each of them had four squads.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. And again, we'll get to some of these topics. If you could please focus on my question. I think we can move on. Now in your statements --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In your statement, Mr. Skrba, you say that: "According to establishment, only the chief of artillery was above me." And if we could clarify a few points here. First, could you explain what you mean by "according to establishment"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a statute and there are rules of the JNA which we inherited as our code of conduct which were in place until we received our own. In a brigade, a chief of artillery is appointed as an expert for artillery pieces in the brigade. He is the most professional or most expert person in those terms, and he is number two man, second only to the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And in your case with the MAD, this chief of artillery at the brigade, that was Mr. Savo Simic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What rank did he hold?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that was at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What was your rank?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So you outranked him, obviously?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was recruited from the reserve complement and he was an active-duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now you explain that -- or, rather, you have explained in testimony in the Karadzic case that towards the end of 1994, you, in addition to your duties as the commander of the MAD, you also took over the duties of the brigade artillery chief on the departure of Mr. Savo Simic. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So from late 1994 onwards, you served as both the brigade artillery chief and also the commander for the MAD?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the beginning of 1995 I discharged both duties. And then in February, March 1995, Dragan Elez was appointed the division commander, whereas I continued serving as the chief of artillery in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification. Now let's take this in stages. First of all, approximately when in late 1994 did you take over the duties of the brigade artillery chief in conjunction with your other dudes as the MAD commander?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date. I believe that it was either in September or October 1994. This is to the best of my recollection. Because Major Simic assumed a new duty in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, up to this point, from the beginning of the war until September or October 1994, who did you receive orders from?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I only received orders from my chief, Simic, or from the brigade commander. Orders and approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, after you took over for Mr. Simic, so when you were dual-headed, so to speak, who did you receive orders from?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards artillery, I got orders from the commander for personnel. As for professional matters, from the chief of artillery from the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And that was -- chief of artillery for the corps, that was Colonel Tadija Manojlovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And Colonel Cvetkovic stood in for him whenever he was absent, and he was absent quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to focus a little bit more on this period when you were either dual-headed, including the role of the brigade artillery chief, or the time after when you were only the brigade artillery chief. My question is: In that role as brigade artillery chief, would it be correct that you were responsible for advising the brigade commander on artillery matters such as, for example, training?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was compulsory information. And every month, at the end of the month or at the beginning of the month, it depended, we would provide monthly reports about our own work and also a plan for the coming month. On the condition that there was no combat, then repairs would be carried out, additional training, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. My question specifically was: You were responsible for advising the brigade commander on training; is that correct? Training for artillery.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the duty was if we would include that in the monthly plan that we would train crews, the commander should know what the subject of the training was and what kind of training was carried out, where, and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you say "we would train crews," it's correct that you, as the brigade artillery chief, organised that kind of training; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, already towards the end of 1994, I became chief as well, then the only thing that could have been done was repetition, making sure that people knew what they knew. They were already three years into the war, and as we say in the military, they should be fit in every conceivable way and they should be properly trained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you organised it, not what was done and whether it was repetition or not, but you, it was your duty to organise that training. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at that moment that was our duty and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's much easier for me to give you answers because your questions are more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'll -- but it's Mr. Shin who is putting clear questions to you. Let me be clear on that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, we will certainly do our best to have --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- very specific questions, and I accept your apology. This monthly plan, you keep talking about "we," but you're the one who is responsible for preparing this monthly plan, even if you had subordinates helping you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Who did you submit this monthly plan to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The monthly plan would be submitted to the brigade command and distributed to the units that were supposed to carry out that plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: As brigade artillery chief, is it correct that you were also responsible for advising the brigade commander about ammunition needs?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was compulsory during our monthly briefings and reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to read you something that Mr. Simic said in another case, and I'll ask you a question about that. He described the brigade artillery chief as including this following function: "In the brigade command, I also provided my input on the use of artillery; i.e., I provided my proposal to the brigade commander. And the brigade commander, at the end of the day, decided whether to accept my proposals or not, or perhaps he had his own suggestions and he would issue orders as to how to place the artillery, how to deploy the assets." Would you agree that that does accurately describe a function of the brigade artillery chief?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is fully correct. This report of his that he made, especially at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And he also said, and I'll quote: "If a combat order was being drafted, I provided my input for the artillery use both verbally and graphically using a map." Would you agree that that also accurately describes one of the functions by the brigade artillery chief?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fully accurate. He is describing the tasks that he carried out, the tasks of artillery chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn next to the issue of the weapons in the MAD. This is something that you were talking about yesterday and just a few minutes ago as well. I just want to make sure that we understood correctly what it was that you had said. First of all, you said that there were three batteries of D30 howitzers, four pieces respectively. So that means 12 pieces in total, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And yesterday the transcript indicated that the D30 is a 120-millimetre howitzer. Is that correct or are they 122-millimetres?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You also said that you had a battery of VBRs, multiple rocket-launchers, four pieces. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you explained that we had two mortar -- I'm sorry, that you had two mortar batteries of 120-millimetre mortars, M-75s, a total of 12 pieces?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: One further point on the D30 howitzer. Now, a D30 howitzer, that designation, that name, refers to a towed [Realtime transcript read in error "TOAD"] weapon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And would it also be correct that this gun -- that this gun could be mounted onto or built into an armoured vehicle, in other words, a self-propelled gun, and that would be known as a gvozdika?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. With the same characteristics like a D30, there are gvozdikas that move on caterpillars, and they are used in the same way and they use the same ammunition but they don't have to be tugged. So vehicles like that don't have to be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if you could have a look at page 31, line 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood you to use a word which I would spell as t-o-w-e-d.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Thank you, Your Honours, and Ms. Stewart had pointed that out as well. I believe that the witness had understood from his answer, so the translators, I believe, got the correct term in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's -- it appears from the answer that that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, did your unit, the MAD, did it have any gvozdikas?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was just at the beginning of the war. Sometime up until the end of May or beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And what happened to those after the end of May, beginning of June?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were taken to the area of Milici, and the others that had been there went to the guard, the guard command, when it was established in Han Pijesak. These were two units with six pieces, respectively, and they had their own assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did the Smbr, apart from the MAD, did the Smbr have any gvozdikas?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any. However, the brigade had 90s from peacetime, but I did not deploy them or command them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And these 90s, what kind of weapon is that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like a tank, a 90-millimetre howitzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So essentially it's a self-propelled 90-millimetre howitzer?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Self-propelled, similar to a tank, but it's 90 millimetres. That's the diameter. Because all these weapons are named on the basis of the diameter of the ammunition that is fired from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you have explained that you did not deploy these 90s or command them. Did -- who in the brigade did command these 90s? We may have an issue with the translation? Is it okay? Okay.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time it was the chief of artillery, Savo Simic, who commanded them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What was the name of the unit that they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, they all got out of my zone of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade. I think that -- that the Drina theatre facing Milici. Now, where they were actually deployed in the Drina Corps, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, you just told us that Savo Simic commanded them and he was the chief of artillery for your brigade.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said he commanded them, I meant that he gave approval and that he was well versed. All of this happened at the beginning of the war in 1992. I think that as chief he knew which unit a particular asset was sent to. He did not command it in terms of using it. He just knew which artillery piece went to which unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: How many 90s are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, it was, say, six or seven. I cannot know the exact number. But as for gvozdikas, I know that there were 11. One battery had six and the other one had five.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you have just told us about weapons, the gvozdikas which you had, as you say, at the beginning of the war and then they went elsewhere. Were there other weapons that you had at the beginning of the war that then went elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rocket-launchers, howitzers, gvozdikas, and these guns, the 90s.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Let's take those one at a time. You've discussed the gvozdikas. How many howitzers that you had at the beginning of the war were then reassigned somewhere else? Just the ones that were reassigned.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the so-called battery gvozdikas that are mobile like tanks. There were two units, one with six and one with five such weapons. The one with six went to Milici and the other one went to prepare in Han Pijesak for the establishment of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. I think I misunderstood your answer but I understand that now. The rockets, how many -- are these, first of all, VBRs also?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had four. However, I had two others that went with the gvozdikas to Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have any other 120 -- you've spoken about the D30s in gvozdika form and you've spoken about the VBRs. Did you have any other 120-millimetre mortars at the beginning of the war that were also sent elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had only two batteries with six mortars, respectively. As far as I know, that's what I got when I assumed that duty in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Can I please have P353 brought on the screen. And I'd like to turn to e-court page English 28 and also in B/C/S 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that to come up, Mr. Skrba, this is General Mladic's notebook entry for the 30th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could please turn to pages 28 in both languages. I'm sorry, can we try page -- is this the correct page? Can we try page 30, please. Okay. Just one moment, please. That's the correct page. I just wanted to make sure that I was giving the right number since I may have moved too quickly for the document to come up in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you see here that these are notes of a meeting between General Mladic and unit commanders of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could please turn to page 30 now. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We're still waiting for the page to come up, Mr. Skrba. Okay. Now you have that there. And under the bottom, in the B/C/S, you see at item number 10 the reference to Lieutenant-Colonel Veljko Stojanovic. Now, he's the commander of the Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now we see the reference here to the two batteries of the gvozdikas that you've been speaking about, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now if we could turn to page E31 and B31.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In the upper third of that page you see a reference to a 1MBNA, 2MB. That's motorised battalion, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the witness is signaling there is a technical issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Can you see the page now, Mr. Skrba?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still have page 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. I understand your confusion then. I'm referring to a technical page number that we have. But yes, you're looking at the right page number if it says "30" on the page. Now, my question, just to remind us, the first -- the reference to the 1MB and the reference to the 2MB, those are references to motorised battalions, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what's written here. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, my question, and perhaps you know the answer to this: The Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade had two armoured battalions, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not two motorised ones. One motorised and -- I'm sorry, I mean, I know that one was motorised and the other one was armoured.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. So one was called a motorised battalion and the other was called an armoured battalion. Now, you see here in General Mladic's entry that the 1st Motorised or Armoured Battalion had ten T-55 tanks. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I am not a technical person, I'm not an armour man, I cannot say. I can't say either yes or no. I mean, it's a differential branch all together. They were just within this brigade. I really cannot say exactly how many of them there were, how many tanks they had, how many APCs. I can neither say yes or no. I just know that one was motorised and the other one was armoured.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, you were the commander of the mixed artillery division. From September or October of 1994, you also held the position of chief of artillery at the brigade. Now, even with artillery and the armoured branches being different fields, are you saying that you did not know what these two armoured or motorised battalions had? Are you saying you did not know that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I do not know because I, in my school for reserve officers, I did not hear such lectures. I did not study their system. I cannot speak about these arms and services when I was not part of that. I served in the artillery. That was what I did as a reserve officer. I was not a professional before the war, and I really don't know how many tanks they had, how many people they had. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You had no factual knowledge of that. So apart from whether you were supposed to know but you -- you also did not know, is that how we have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Correct. This information I received during the briefings at the brigade command when the commanders of these units reported there, and I remember that in passing or something that I needed for defence or attack. However, I did not go into the technical details because I am not professionally versed in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you didn't know about ten tanks in the 1st Motorised Battalion, you had no idea whether there was one or 20?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, I just know the establishment that one was motorised and the other one was armoured. I just know what the establishment was. But how many pieces they had, how many units they had. I really don't know. I was not trained for that, I was not in charge of that, and I was not trained for that particular service in the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have also had not by any chance heard something about it or -- even if it was not your responsibility. Sometimes I do know things or I hear things which are beyond my duties. Did you ever hear the strength of those, the armament of those battalions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know that this armoured battalion went to Grbavica, and how many weapons they had I don't know. But I think that it was deployed. I mean, that's what I seem to remember from the briefings, that there was a company at Grbavica. And where the others were, I don't know. I mean, it was just through these monthly briefings that I would find out where certain units were and whether they were acting in co-ordination with me for some particular operation. Things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, I'm going to focus on something you said a little while ago and repeated just now, that you learned about these units during briefings at the brigade command. And now that's what I want to ask you about, not what you learned about in the military academy or in any school. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clear. Anything I learned at a meeting or that I know otherwise I can confirm, as I did before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, let's take that step by step. First, in these meetings you learned that each of these battalions, this motorised or armoured battalion, had T-55 tanks, at least one; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You also learned that they had BVP armoured vehicles; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You also learned that they had M80s; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that. I didn't hear that. I couldn't show you that they had M80s.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: But you do know what an M80 is; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know what M80 means. I know M82, that's a mortar. I don't know what M80 is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And an M82 would be an 82-millimetre mortar as you described earlier. Now, another thing --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's part of my specialty, the artillery. That's why I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Your specialty is artillery. You've told us that. Now, you've also said a little while ago that you heard about these units, for example, in the context of whether they were "needed for defence or attack," and also in the context of whether they would be "co-ordinated" with you. Now, isn't it true that there were times when you co-ordinated the activities of the MAD with the activities of one or both of these battalions, motorised or armoured?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, such situations didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So when you were saying that you may have heard of these in the context of needing them for defence or attack or for co-ordination, that just never happened? You were just saying that as a hypothetical?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skrba, in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- you say that the chain of command was never bypassed, and you explain also that the principle of subordination was observed. My question to you is whether that would mean -- whether we should understand that to mean that orders went from the corps to the brigades with the expectation that they would be obeyed. That's just the principle of command and control; right? Orders go from the command -- from the corps to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And from the brigade to the battalion or -- and in your field, from the brigade to the MAD and so on?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And when you talk about the chain of command and the principle of subordination, you're also referring to the fact that above the corps, the corps reports to the commander of the Main Staff. That's clear, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's standard practice in all armies. One command reports to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move now to an issue you've discussed previously. That's the issue of your firing positions. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, could I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- still seek clarification?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read to you what you said a while ago when asked about your knowledge about those battalions. You said: "I mean, it was just through these monthly briefings that I would find out where certain units were and whether they were acting in co-ordination with me for some particular operation. Things like that." I understood this as that you -- that such events happened, that it happened that they, meaning one or the two of these battalions, were acting in co-ordination with you because how would you otherwise find out during a briefing if it never happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at the briefing itself. At the brigade command, we briefed each of us about our own problems and the responsibilities we had, the tasks we had to carry out with the units on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you said "whether they were acting in co-ordination with me," so that -- I understood that to be that during those briefings that you were reporting on actions or operations which took place in a co-ordinated way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those co-ordinated modes of action were stable because our unit never tried during the whole war to launch an attack, an advance, and then retreat. We spent the entire war in the same firing positions, and our infantry in front of us was 95 per cent on the same positions all the time. So regarding a certain elevation, we decided that, first of all, I would attack and then perhaps the armoured battalion would continue, et cetera. In that sense we co-ordinated and received instructions from the command during the briefings. Who would assist first or who had better visibility, in that sense we co-ordinated in response to an enemy attack should it happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, we were on the issue of your firing positions. But let me just ask you one question about what you've just said. You said that some of these discussions were about whether first you would attack and then perhaps the armoured battalion would continue. Doesn't that mean you were co-ordinating your actions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first, as the superior in MAD, I received information from the observation points that could see the enemy. I would receive a report that a certain feature was attacked, I would pass that on to the command, and the command would then tell me whether I would act first or some other unit. If I get approval from them, then I would fire at the source of that fire and then the infantry would go on to keep that ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, you do appreciate that the Judge's question was about during those briefings and that is what you were answering, not a question about what was happening in the field with your observers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My observers reported to me and I reported to the command that in a certain sector of the firing line such and such a thing was happening, and then I awaited instructions from them, who would return fire first, who would react first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'll move on. We were going to discuss your firing positions. And I wanted to see if we understood accurately your evidence so far about your firing positions. Now, first of all, you explained that all your firing positions were 300 metres from your command post and you marked the map. Just so we're clear on this, I would like to go to a more detailed map that you marked during your Karadzic testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 30675.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, while we're waiting for that to come up -- yeah, we have it now. Do you recognise this as a map that you marked during your testimony in the Karadzic case? That, for example, is your signature, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, I think we resumed one hour ago. If you -- if it takes more than two or three minutes, I would rather save it until after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: It's a bit difficult for me to estimate, but I think it would be more than two or three minutes for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think we first should take a break and then we will resume at 12.00, but we'll only take the break after the witness has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to come in, I already can announce that our next break will be a little bit longer than usual, that will be from 1.00 to 1.30. So half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, I see you have your glasses and we were actually about to look at a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could please have 65 ter 306 -- 6 -- I'm sorry, let me try that again, 30675 on the screen. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, I believe, Mr. Skrba, you had confirmed that that's your signature there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now if you could please explain to the Court -- well, let me put it to you this way: At the top -- in the middle at the top we see two red lines sort of converging on each other. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Those are two red lines that you drew to indicate two firing positions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, below that we see two marks over a place that, if we zoom in a little bit, we can see is Uzdojnice. Did you intend by that to indicate the location of your command post?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the location of the command post where we were throughout the war and where the observers were with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, further below we see two other lines and would it be correct that those two lines also indicate two firing positions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were the positions of the howitzers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I think you're anticipating my questions. If we could start with the upper left of these four lines -- red lines you've drawn, could you tell us what you had at each of those firing positions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These first two upper lines were mortars, 120-millimetres, six weapons. The next one just below the command, these straight lines were the firing positions of howitzers, 100-D30, 122-millimetres, they had six weapons each. So two firing positions, six weapons each.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then seek clarification for -- you said the mortars, 120-millimetres, six weapons, is that for one or for the two together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said these two lines are two positions of mortars, 120-millimetres, M75. On one line there were six weapons and on the other line there were six weapons also. So two batteries with 120-millimetre weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the lines, do they indicate in which direction they were usually oriented or -- I mean, the howitzers are in parallel, the other weapons are in a kind of a V shape. Could you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This lower line going towards the command post was the position of the 120-millimetre battery. They were facing north towards Zlatiste, the Jewish cemetery, et cetera; and the other line was facing Ozrenska Street, Lukavica, the Cica barracks, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that would be westerly direction rather than north?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't have a compass here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's clear to me now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, just to follow-up on the Judge's questions, you told us you did not have a compass. You were in this area the entire war, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You know where Lukavica is.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Are you telling this Court that you need a compass to decide what direction it is from these firing positions to Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the Karadzic case you testified that these four positions were permanent and they did not move until August 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And these firing positions you've marked, this is where they were when you took command on the 27th of May, 1992, of the MAD; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move on to the topic of command posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, one more. The mortars, they are just lines, they are parallel lines, but are they oriented towards the north-east or to the south-west? A line has a beginning and an end. Is it direction of town or is it ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your question. I just roughly drew these lines indicating six weapons. The upper line was facing west and the lower line was facing north. The lower line was facing Zlatiste and the upper line was facing Debelo Brdo, Mojmilo, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're explaining now the mortars. I was asking now about the howitzers which are the two lines further down. Were they directed north-east or were they directed in the opposite direction, south-west?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was new equipment. With those howitzers I was able to fire 360 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, we were discussing your command post. You've already explained where that is. Now, you testified in the Karadzic case that Uzdojnice was also the command post of other units that were deployed there. Can you tell us what these other units were that were deployed there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this area between the howitzer firing positions there is a little black dot here. Even before the war there was a communications company there, a signals company. They kept their communications equipment between our firing positions. If necessary, I'll mark it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Let's see whether we need to do that. You mentioned that -- in the Karadzic case you said that Uzdojnice was a command post of other units, in the plural, that were deployed there. Apart from this communications unit, what other units were deployed there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no one there except for my battery. Maybe I meant in that passage that the commands of these batteries were deployed there. That's what I meant and that's how it was, 100 per cent sure. Apart from this signals company, there were no military or technical units there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: This signals company, by the way, was that a company under what superior command?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That company was under the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30675 receives number P6519, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6519 is admitted into evidence and it was marked in the previous case. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: To continue on, Mr. Skrba, with this issue of -- this topic of the command post, I would like to turn to another map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could I please have 65 ter 30674 brought to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, while we're waiting for that to come up, let me just anticipate that by saying it is another map that you marked during your testimony in the Karadzic case. Do you recognise this map and do you recognise that signature to be yours?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, we see in the middle of this map Uzdojnice again, which, as you've explained, was your command post. Now, to the left of that and a little bit to the south we see a mark - if we could zoom in a little bit - another red circle that's been drawn over a place named Pavlovac. Now, you said in the Karadzic case that this indicated the command of a subordinate unit, a unit subordinated to you. What subordinate command was that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not a unit subordinated to us. This was the command post of my brigade. We were subordinated to that brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. So that is a command post, that red mark to the left, that is a command post of the Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now continuing on with this map, if we look to the right, you've also made a mark at a place named Tilava. And in the Karadzic case, you testified that there was an infirmary and a local commune there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Maybe for completeness before I tender this, could you explain to the Judges what marks -- what those marks in the upper left of this map indicate?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They asked me about Energoinvest and the electrical engineering faculty. Energoinvest is a famous company and next to it is the electrical engineering school of the university.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So would it be correct that IE refers to Energoinvest and ETF refers to the faculty?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30674 receives number P6520, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skrba, I'd like to continue on to a slightly different topic. In your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- you described the establishment of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, and there you note that it was formed from the remaining hardware and personnel from the JNA. You add that it consisted mostly of hardware and was insufficiently manned, and you've addressed that topic earlier today. Just so we're clear, isn't it true that at the outset of the war the MAD, in particular, had the largest number of active officers and soldiers among SRK artillery units?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct and I claim that with full responsibility. Not a single officer in the MAD was an active officer, with the exception of Chief Savo Simic, who was an artillery specialist. There were some active lieutenants, but they left with the units that went to Milici. The area that we have just discussed and the deployment of those units, after the JNA left, they didn't leave behind any career officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Let's look at a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could I please have P4435.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, while we're waiting for that document to come up, let me explain what it is. This is a Sarajevo Romanija Corps command analysis of the combat readiness of corps artillery rocket units. It's dated, as you can see on the front page, July 1994. We can go to the back later to see that it's signed by chief of artillery, Colonel Tadija Manojlovic, and we've already discussed him. Just one quick question, as chief of artillery at the SRK, Colonel Manojlovic was a member of the SRK command staff, was he not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What command staff are you talking about? He was part of the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, that was exactly my question. Thank you. Now, one other preliminary question here: The phrase "artillery rocket units of the SRK," what does that include specifically?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the chief of artillery in the corps command, this comprises all artillery units at lower levels. And we are talking about batteries, divisions, regiments, depending on the specialty of the weapons that he had and disposed with. The lower units are brigades and they can also be independent artillery regiments with their own specific types of weapons. Regiments are the level of the -- of the brigade in terms of establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And following on from your explanation, it would be correct that the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment was one of these units, it was a corps asset?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment? I'm not familiar with that. Maybe you misspoke or maybe the terminology is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Let me try the designation that's used in the VRS, the 4th MAP?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, a MAP is an entirely different thing. It's a mixed artillery regiment and it's mixed because it has different weapons of different calibre. It should have been called a division, but when there is a designation "mixed," that means that the type of weaponry varies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the linguistical problem has been resolved. Was the 4th MAP, was that one of the units -- was it a corps asset? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you were describing the designation "mixed." Your unit was also a mixed artillery unit, so clearly the 4th Mixed Artillery, from your description, would also have 120-millimetre mortars, correct, among other things?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regiment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, I think we've resolved that, it's the MAP and the P stands for "puk" which means "regiment."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a regiment is a unit at a higher level than a division, and in terms of establishment, it does not belong to a brigade. It is at the corps level. And I'm just explaining why they were mixed, because a regiment has units with artillery weapons with bigger barrels. They don't have 120-millimetre mortars, their howitzers or cannons, 130. The higher level unit, the higher the establishment level, which implies that they have higher calibre artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: But the corps did have 120-millimetre mortars; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about their establishment. They were quite far away from me. They were in Pale. They were not on my left flank or on my right flank. They were not in my area of responsibility. I never co-operated with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, you were the chief of artillery for the Smbr, the Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, from September, October 1994 onwards. But you had no idea whether the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, your immediately superior command, had any 120-millimetre mortars? You had no idea. Not whether they did or not whether they didn't. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I claim: I don't know what their composition was. Just having passed through their deployment lines, I can't tell you what they had -- or, rather, I didn't see any mortars. Maybe they had them or maybe not. I can't say that for a fact. They never informed me and I never attended any meetings at the corps level. I never heard any of their briefings, therefore there is no way for me to know what they had at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you have any impression? Did you ever receive any information on what they might have had? Even if it was not official information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
