utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. This is what I said. There were 150 and 105 howitzers. I knew the commander, Dragoljub Tosic, I knew him from before the war. He was the commander of that regiment. But I was not aware of his detailed composition. I know that they had VBRs, 128, but I was not aware of a more precise composition of the unit. We were not in contact. We never discussed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And mortars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I can't say either yes or no. In terms of establishment, they were not supposed to have mortars, but I'm not claiming that they didn't. But I was never officially informed about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You earlier said: "I don't know anything about their establishment." And in your last answer you say: "In terms of establishment, they were not supposed to have mortars ..." So therefore do you have any knowledge about their establishment or do you not have any knowledge about the establishment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time you tell us that they are supposed not to have mortars, according to their establishment. If you don't know anything, how could you know, then, that they are supposed not to have mortars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I served in the JNA, we had manoeuvres, and I remember from that what a division should have had as opposed to a regiment. I remember what the composition of a regiment was as opposed to a composition of a division. And based on those manoeuvres, I can tell that regiment never had mortars. It always had higher calibre weapons with a longer range, and their calibre was 100-millimetre, 150-millimetre, and then they were mixed regiment. If it was a uniform regiment, it had a higher calibre. And now on to a division. A division usually has four batteries in terms of establishment -- or, rather, it has three batteries with the same weapons. And if it's a mixed division, if it has mortars, then it can be called a mixed artillery division or a mixed artillery regiment if it is a formation at a higher level. That means that their artillery pieces are mixed, that there is a variety.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, maybe one more question on what the -- the explanation you've been providing the Court. Now, you were aware -- you've mentioned a couple of things that you believe the corps had, VBRs, howitzers, but can you tell us - and perhaps you have, it's not clear to me - whether you were aware that the corps had 120-millimetre mortars, whether in the 4th MAP or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps had mortars and they were deployed among the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I will move on. Now we were looking at this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could please go to page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now we can see, Mr. Skrba, at the bottom half of this page, in the first sentence under number 1, command and control, we can see that this report covers two periods: From the beginning of the war to 20th May 1992; and secondly, from that date on to July 1994. A little below it reads: "The MAD/1st Smbr, which was a component of the 4th Corps, had in their ranks the largest number of active officers and soldiers which facilitated the combat assignments to be carried out in the area of responsibility of both the 1st Smbr and the Corps." Now, I want to ask you about the first part of that. Isn't it correct, as Colonel Manojlovic has written here, that your unit, the MAD, had, among the SRK artillery rocket units, the largest number of active officers and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that. Only the chief of artillery up to September, October was an active officer in the MAD. The rest of us were reservists. I can give you the names of the commanders who had all joined from the reserve complement. And as for Mr. Manojlovic, who said that, I would like to hear him say that. I know that he could not write that. But it is true that the Sarajevo Brigade had most of the professional officers but they were deployed elsewhere. They were assigned to other units, not to the MAD.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, perhaps in that regard, we can focus on the second part of that sentence. Isn't it correct that, as Colonel Manojlovic writes, that the MAD "facilitated the combat assignments to be carried out in the area of responsibility of both the 1st Smbr and of the SRK"? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where does it say that? However, wherever it says that, I don't know how he could claim that. I don't know what the essence of the question was. We performed our tasks within the brigade, and if the brigade received an order, like I just told you a while ago when we had only two batteries with six weapons, and then we had three batteries with four batteries [as interpreted], and then we would send our unit 20 kilometres away if there was a task that took them there. Maybe that was an advantage of the mobile unit. Maybe that was the rationale behind him saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So as you're explaining, it appears that Colonel Manojlovic was correct that the MAD could be sent 20 kilometres away, which means certainly outside of the Smbr's zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It does not mean that it was outside of the zone of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, but in any case, it was outside of the zone that stretches 20 kilometres from the centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I see. I think I may have misunderstood your earlier answer. Now, did the MAD do this -- facilitate combat assignments in the SRK's zone of responsibility but outside the Smbr's zone of responsibility? Did that occur throughout the entire war or what time-period did that occur?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened every now and then and it depended on the enemy attacks, where our lines of defence were attacked. Those were specific situations, especially after 1994 up until the end of 1994 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So we can understand that to mean, as you're referring to 1994 and 1995, that was also true in 1992 and 1993? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So that was true only in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the Lukavac 93, we gained a lot of manoeuvre positions so we could move away from Sarajevo, 20 kilometres from the centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn to the Smbr itself. You've previously testified that mortars under the size of 120-millimetres, they were with the infantry battalions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So 82-millimetre mortars, for example, were with the battalions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: How many 82-millimetre mortars did the 2nd Battalion have?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they had four.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What about the other infantry battalions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Infantry Battalion also had either three or four pieces. And the 1st also had either three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What about mortars of smaller size?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are 60-millimetre mortars which are carried on one's back. I don't know how many there were and where they were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. I'll now move on to a slightly different topic. I may return to that one as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 30641. But, I'm sorry, just before we do that, could we look at the last page of this document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, you recognise the signature of Colonel Manojlovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see his name but I'm really not familiar with his signature. He was not my superior officer before the war and throughout the war he was at the corps command all the time, so I really don't know what his signature looks like. I suppose that this may be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So we'll move on to 65 ter 30641, please. And, Your Honours, this is a detail from a map from P3. And we saw one detail -- a slightly different detail yesterday and now we're seeing this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skrba, this map doesn't show the full area of the 1st Smbr's zone of responsibility as in a map that had been tendered earlier during your testimony. But you see the dotted red and blue lines. That's the line of confrontation, correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now if we look to the bottom and a little bit to the left of centre, you see a thinner red line in dashes and dots, and you can see the Zeljeznica river; correct? Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, this line with dots and dashes on it, this would mark the left side of the brigade's zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And would it be correct - and I believe you have this in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- that the neighboring unit is the 2nd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 2nd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade is on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And if we look to the right side of this map but still under the portion on the right side that has the blue and red confrontation line, you see once again a thinner red line with dots and dashes, and that would be the right side of the Smbr's zone of responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And the neighbouring unit there was the 1st Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you spoke earlier today about Trebevic and you were telling this Court that the ABiH were firing at you from Trebevic. We can see Trebevic, the word is appearing just roughly parallel to that thin red line with dashes and dots. It's pretty clear on this map, isn't it, that Trebevic is held by the VRS, first?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lines depict the VRS positions on the left and on the right. I don't understand your question, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, we see the word "Trebevic" and that entire word appears within the SRK side of the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Parts of Trebevic stretch all the way to the bed of the Miljacka river and to the highway. I believe that a scale of this map is 1:50.000 which is why things seem the way they are. They were at the initial positions along the elevated parts of Trebevic, especially around Zlatiste, on the end on Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could we zoom in on this map a little bit, please, and move over to -- so that we can centre the word "Trebevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, we can see -- you're talking about the Miljacka river, and you've just told us that Trebevic includes areas that go right down to the bank of the Miljacka river. Now, we see the Miljacka river projecting in a direction towards the south-east from the lower right corner of the confrontation line; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now that part, of course, is under VRS control.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That part around the Miljacka river was not at all under the VRS control, starting with Kozja Cuprija.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And I believe we can see what you're talking about there, Kozja Cuprija. But if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should avoid touching the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I see whether -- you talked about Zlatiste and Trebevic. Do you consider Zlatiste to be part of Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, both Zlatiste and Debelo Brdo below Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could we find Zlatiste on this map. Let's have a look. I have difficulties in finding it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This term "Grad" and "Vranjac," this is actually Zlatiste. There is a fortress there. That is why the area is called "Grad" or "fortress." And the general area around these two places is known as Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you again clearly indicate where you found "Grad" and -- because I have not found it yet. Is it on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, between Debelo Brdo and Vranjac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is Vranjac indicated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between those two. Yes, it is indicated on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could someone help me to find it. Mr. Shin, if you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry, I'm struggling to find it as well. It's possible that the word "Grad" does not appear on this map and we may be able to assist with another one, unless my colleague Mr. Stojanovic can assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, where do we find ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, if you can follow the irregular rectangle in the left upper corner of the big rectangle, it is right below the red line where it says "Grad," "Vranjac" and "Debelo Brdo." Well, this area is also part of Trebevic known as Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now found Debelo Brdo, which is indicated as an elevation 745, which is situated on this map just between the VRS and the opposite army. Then I find "Grad" and "Vranjac" just south of that, and that seems not to be within the area controlled by the forces opposing the VRS. So on this map at least it's not clearly Muslim-controlled or Presidency-controlled area. And at the same time I also notice that apparently the witness defines what Trebevic is different from just the words as we find them on the map. May I take it that he is referring to the lower part of the slopes of that -- what I think is a mountain. And therefore, I think whenever we are talking about firing from Trebevic or from elsewhere that we should be more precise in finding the locations the witness is referring to exactly. Could you keep this in mind, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just one more question on this map, Mr. Skrba. You see the word "Trebevic" on this map. Would you agree at least that the word "Trebevic" is written over an area that is known as Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And that area of Trebevic is in the zone of responsibility of the 1st Romanija Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, its northern part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And in fact you see that flag just above the V in Trebevic with the four on it. That would be -- that would indicate the command post of the 4th Battalion of the 1st Romanija Brigade; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. For the record, on two occasions it was recorded "the 1st Romanija Brigade." This may cause confusion. Did the Prosecutor have in mind the Romanija Brigade or the Sarajevo Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I believe the witness has told us that to the right side of this dotted and dashed red line under Trebevic, that's where the Romanija Brigade was. I think that's in the record --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- and he's just confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So, Mr. Skrba, we will move on but I want to stay with this map. Now, my colleague, Mr. Stojanovic, has pointed to a feature about this irregular rectangular shape that we see in almost the centre of this map. Now, to help orient you, this roughly rectangular shape has in the centre of it in Cyrillic letters the acronym BRAG. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now BRAG means brigade artillery group, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And a brigade artillery group, could you tell me if this would be correct: That that's a formation which was made up by combining different components of the brigade assets to form an artillery group for a -- as a temporary structure for a specific action?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And that's the same concept that applies at the corps level, right? And the letters KAG would signify a corps artillery group?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear, on the English channel, I hear on the background the B/C/S interpretation. I don't know what causes it. No one would expect me to be bilingual, I think, but let's proceed and see whether it can be fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So, Mr. Skrba, we were discussing the brigade artillery groups, and you had explained -- you had agreed with me what the nature of those are. Now, in this particular map, this brigade artillery group encompasses the two positions you've outlined before in Uzdojnice and one position further south; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: It also encompasses these two positions further up closer to the confrontation line. Now, those would be weapons of infantry --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: The witness -- I believe you said "tocna;" is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hear the question to the end. I was interrupted -- or the interpretation was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That's likely my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We see at the upper end of this roughly rectangular shape that there are two -- two diagrams, and this would represent weapons of the battalion -- infantry battalions; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Whose weapons would those be?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those would be of a motorised or an armoured battalion that were both on the strength of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. So these would be assets of the motorised or armoured battalions that you discussed earlier?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So you're sure that that's what these are? You didn't appear to know very much about them earlier.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the drawing, I can see that those were assets on tanks and those were the tanks that were on the strength of either the armoured or the motorised battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Indeed. So the armoured and motorised battalions each had tanks and that's what you believe these are. Now, this indicates that you did have co-ordinated actions between your positions and the actions -- and the battalions, whether armoured or motorised; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had co-ordinated actions if we were attacked. That's why you can see where they should be deployed in case of attack. If we came under attack, we could defend ourselves. That's why they were here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So even though you co-ordinated actions with these armoured or motorised brigades -- I'm sorry, battalions, you actually didn't know what they had?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I only saw when a tank, T-55, arrived, because I was familiar with that. I was not familiar with any of the other technical equipment that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm going to move on. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you do so, I think it's 1.00. Mr. Shin, it's time --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry, I missed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have the slightly longer break. Could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom. We take a break of half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 1.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, according to my calculations or, rather, Madam Registrar's calculations, you have one hour left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honours. Let me just check with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, two hours left. My calculations are -- what I added was wrong. Two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Your Honours. I thought there may have been an issue there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, there is no issue. You may proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, we were -- when we left off we were discussing the brigade artillery group. Now, could you explain to this Court who it was who had proposed the formation of a brigade artillery group?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before me, Captain Savo Simic made that proposal, and after that that was me, but there was no need for me to hand this over because we were already involved in this war for over two years. But anyway, that was my proposal when I became chief in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And who would you make your proposal to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we made that proposal to the commander and then he would accept it or correct it or refuse it. And then we'd ask for approval from the superior command from the corps, according to subordination from the chief of artillery of the corps, to see whether he would agree with such a proposal, this kind of deployment, and so on. So it would be the brigade command that would have to ask for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, upon the formation of a brigade artillery group, who would command such a formation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, it would be the chief of artillery, along with the order and approval of the brigade commander and these subordinate units that became a part of those brigades or that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So with the chief of artillery being the person who would command the formation, that would have been you after September or October of 1994?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, in a related area, we've already discussed the fact that the infantry battalions did not have 120-millimetre mortars. Now, when an infantry battalion required heavier support than an 82-millimetre mortar, who would they make that request to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the MAD command that would have to be asked or the command of the brigade, and then the commander of the brigade would perhaps ask the MAD command to see what should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Was it possible for a battalion commander to contact you directly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if so approved by the brigade command for him to communicate with me directly for that particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And in such cases, then you would be able to use any of the weapons at your disposal as you believed in your professional judgement would be appropriate?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. To see what are the weapons involved, what are the positions involved, so how I could protect my positions by involving that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm a little confused by your last answer. My question has been not -- my questions have been not about protecting your positions with infantry units but rather your support for battalions. And, in fact, that's why we were discussing the battalions contacting you and not the other way around.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, us, but I support infantry battalions in order to preserve our defence lines. Throughout the war we never went out to attack the city. That is why I'm saying this is support to defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And that kind of support could occur from your 120-millimetre mortars, of course; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that mortars are anti-personnel weapons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it depends on the type of attack involved. If the infantry is out to attack and is fighting outside trenches, they become a legal military objective because they are attacking our soldiers on the first line of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. The question was whether mortars are anti-personnel weapons, not whether troops were legal military objectives because what they did, but are mortars anti-personnel weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if the attacks go directly against the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We were not talking about attacks. We were talking about the characteristics of a weapon. Is it an anti-personnel weapon or is it anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an artillery piece that is used for destroying the infantry in different cases. Let me not repeat what I've already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the answer is it's an anti-personnel weapon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, I'm going to move to a slightly different area now. Now, in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- you say that you were "very satisfied with the precision of our fire and the training level of the MAD personnel." I'd like to ask you a little further about this. You expanded on the targeting part of this process in your Karadzic testimony. Among other things, you said: "Every target had to be marked and described in terms of its size, location, and what kind of enemy assets were there, whether there was manpower or equipment and everything else." You stand by your evidence in the Karadzic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You explain further that: "We always expected specific information, the location, the place, and the size of the target." And you stand by that as well?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You were asked in the Karadzic case why these details were important to you, and you answered: "Those details are important so that we should be able to plan what kind of artillery we should open, individual fire with one weapon or group fire with a whole unit using weapons of a specific calibre." And you stand by that as well?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You also mention that you received orders only in writing. Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on what happened, whether an attack was carried out. If that happened, then there wasn't enough time to write this up. Then through communications equipment there would have to be agreement. Of course, we're not going to wait for an order to be written. I would inform the brigade command and the brigade command would inform me. They would give me their agreement for me to proceed so that I would protect the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So, in fact, contrary to what you had testified in Karadzic, you did receive verbal orders?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, in your Karadzic testimony, you were asked what the procedure would be for challenging an order. You explain that you would ask for written approval and you explained: "... I always made sure through my observers and artillery observers, our people on our forward lines on higher ground who did reconnaissance and scouting, if they gave me a report and assurance what kind of target that was, only then could an order be issued to prepare fire and open fire." You stand by that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, these artillery observers, could you please explain to the Court where they were, your artillery observers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our artillery observers were in our -- or, rather, behind our front line in the area of Zlatiste, then up there at Vrace, and towards Ozrenska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, when you say your "observers," could you explain to us were they part of your unit, the MAD?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were part of the MAD or, rather, part of the units that were within the MAD.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you also receive targeting information from observers who were attached to the corps?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not get any orders from them, no reconnaissance, nothing. It's not that we had common observation posts so that we could co-ordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, even though you didn't have common observation posts, you never received any information from the corps observers; is that right? Targeting information.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In the Karadzic case, you were also asked how many times you would fire from a 120-millimetre mortar, and you said: "Only rarely would it be one shell." Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'd like to move to a slightly different area now, also relating to your Karadzic testimony. Mr. Skrba, in that testimony you described locations that you did not target; specifically, you said: "Hospitals, bus stations, railway stations and rail lines, schools, and all the areas where larger groups of civilians tend to gather, those were the facilities that we did not target." Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You were also asked what you meant by "all the areas where larger groups of civilians tend to gather," and your answer was: "I was born and raised there, so I knew where bus stops were, where tram stations were, big supermarkets where people went to get their supplies, and wherever the frequency of the civilian population was quite high, those were the areas that we did not expose to fire."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You further testified that you would not fire within 1 kilometre of a hospital. You stand by that as well?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by that. Since I was born in Sarajevo, I know exactly what the buildings are and I would not wish any harm. I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, indeed, in connection with what you just said, you were asked in Karadzic also whether you took these -- that you avoided these targets because you did not want to potentially kill any civilians. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we tried to avoid these targets. We didn't want to hit them and we managed to avoid that 99 per cent, at least from my positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And specifically you were asked in the Karadzic case whether there were any circumstances whether you would have accepted the risk of civilians death in connection with these types of targets, and you said: "Even in such cases, I wouldn't open fire if I thought that the civilian population was at risk." And you stand by that as well?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now you discuss further in your Karadzic testimony -- well, let me back up a minute and say in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- Mr. Skrba, you use a phrase "proportionate fire," and you describe a situation where if fire came from a tank, you would respond with tank fire. Is that what you mean by proportionate fire?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mean responding with the same calibre. That's impossible. I meant proportionately. If from Ciglana or Hum a tank fires one or two shells and then continues, then I just respond with one or two shells. I mean, I'm just speaking about the same proportion, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. So if you were attacked you would respond proportionately. Now --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Proportionately also to neutralise them so that they do not fire at our positions further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Moving a little bit away, as we are now, from civilian targets, we were just talking about targeting a tank. If you had a road, a communication road that was away from civilian areas, it would be permissible, wouldn't it, to use fire to control that road to prevent the enemy from using that road?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, that primarily pertained to the tank at Hum which was underneath the relay station, and there were no more civilians there, and it was moving from one place to another and firing from there specifically.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last part of your answer which was not caught by the interpreters. You said: "... and there were no more civilians there, and it was moving from one place to another and firing from there specifically." What did you then say after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that tank would usually be fired at so that I would neutralise it so that it would not open fire at us. The tank was only hiding at different places that had already been prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, continuing, what I was explaining to you is a situation where it's not a civilian area. If you wanted to prevent your enemy from getting access to, let's say, a communication road, you would be able to use fire to control that road to prevent the enemy from using that road. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's moving, then I would fire at it. I don't have a lot of ammunition, so I have none to spare. I don't have enough ammunition to keep targeting something without having a particular specific target.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Skrba, I think the confusion is mine. This is a -- I'm explaining a situation where there is no tank involved. The situation is as follows: If you have a road, a communications road far away from civilian areas, it is legitimate, is it not, to use artillery to fire on the road and control access to it so that the enemy will not use it. Will that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But there weren't any such situations and I never opened fire in such moments because our ammunition supply was limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on now. Mr. Skrba, in another part of your testimony in the Karadzic case you were asked about air bombs. Now, you testified in that case that: "Aerial bombs have a lot of power. They're heavier, they have more projectiles. If a shell is heavy, some 50 to 70 kilogrammes, and if the aerial bomb is heavy, from 3- to 500 kilogrammes, of course it has a lot of lethal power, a lot of destructive power, and of course one cannot be sure to hit the centre." Do you stand by that testimony in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by that. But these air bombs, as far as I know, they weighed from 150 to 250 kilogrammes, not more than that. And for them there had to be special training. But in my unit we never did that. I personally was not involved in that either because we had not been trained to use such assets. In order to be able to use something like that and to fire something like that, you'd have to have it in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You continued in the Karadzic case on this topic, and I'll read what you said. "If you fire a shell and then you can vouch for hitting the target within 50 metres, in the case of an aerial bomb, it would be 500 metres because it's much -- it's a much bigger projectile." You stand by that as well?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think so. We were actually taught that, that a mine shell has one diameter but air bombs have a much larger diameter. I never fired them, though, and I could never then go and see what it was like when it would be fired. This was never done in peacetime, and I would just logically make an assumption, that it's a stronger explosion and that the effect is therefore greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now moving on to another topic, Mr. Skrba, yesterday in court and in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- Mr. Skrba, you say that the SRK was in a double encirclement, an inner and an outer one. I want to look at a map and see if we can understand better what it is you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could we please have P3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting for that map --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- could I seek clarification of one of the previous answers. You were asked, Mr. Skrba, about an answer you gave in the Karadzic case. You said: "If you can fire a shell and then you can vouch for hitting the target within 50 metres, in the case of an aerial bomb, it would be 500 metres because it's a much bigger projectile." Now, later on in your answers you were telling us that the explosion was far heavier, which would have a stronger effect. But this answer given in the Karadzic case seems to relate to the precision of hitting the target. Do I have to understand that testimony that apart from the bomb, or perhaps that being the reason, apart from the bomb being far bigger, that also the precision in firing is far less compared to another projectile?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stand by the first part, what I said, 50 metres. That is a 120-millimetre mortar. And the rest, that's correct. Once the correction is made that -- a target can be engaged. 50 metres -- yes, well, that is with a simple artillery preparation, to put it in the briefest possible terms. I don't know what elements they took into account as far as air bombs were concerned and what the assets were. Also when it says "air bomb," I would assume that they would have used aircraft for that, helicopters. But I don't know -- since it was a no-fly zone, I don't know how they fired this, but the very logic of it says that if it weighs 150 kilogrammes or 250 kilogrammes, that it's heavier, that it has a bigger diameter. And, of course, since it's so big and heavy it is harder to have a high degree of precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so I understood that when you referred to 500 metres, you were referring to a far worse precision in hitting a target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said 500 metres, that had to do only with the following: Those who were launching a shell, an air bomb, that it can kill within 500 metres. And now what the precision is, it may be 100 per cent and it can also have a deviation of 50 metres from the actual place that they had targeted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then I'm confused by your previous answer. But I'll allow Mr. Shin to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Shin, do you want to tender Exhibit 65 ter 30641 or are you not tendering?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, you have anticipated the point I was going to make. If I could, before we go to this map, tender the previous document, which was 65 ter 30641, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30641 receives number P6521, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could I please have e-court page 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, this is going to be a map, I believe. Let's make sure I have that page right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you have the page number of the hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, it's e-court page -- I'm sorry, no, I don't. I do -- I do have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you don't, don't worry, I will find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm told it's usually six less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Skrba, you see the map on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could stay right there without going in any further magnification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, that circle that you see -- well, first of all, near the centre of the -- or, rather, if we look at the circle on the left at what would be around 2.00, do you see the Cyrillic letters SRK?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And that would include a portion of the zone of responsibility of the SRK; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And do we see the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps off to the right? And if we look, continuing on a 2.00 direction from SRK we see the Cyrillic letters DK?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the demarcation line between the Sarajevo Corps and the Drina Corps is clearly marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So that's what that red line indicates, it's a demarcation line between the two corps.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now within that circle that we've been looking at, you can recognise, perhaps, the larger map from which our previous map came, and you can see the dotted or dashed blue and red lines indicating the line of confrontation between the ABiH and the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just one more question on this. On the other side of the Drina Corps, wouldn't that lead towards Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't see it on the map here. And it's true, on the right hand side of the Drina is Serbia, but you can't see it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, in what sense is SRK in a double encirclement, looking at this map?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map is clearly drawn after the Lukavac 93 operation and that was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We'll address the Lukavac 93 operation a little later on, but hasn't the Drina Corps always been holding an area contiguous to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every corps was in its own place. The Sarajevo Romanija Corps is here on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. Mr. Skrba, isn't it clear that the Drina Corps and the Sarajevo Romanija Corps always held adjacent areas of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they were much closer to this internal circle where you see the letters SRK, of about 90 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I see. Now, Lukavac 93 was about the Herzegovina Corps, wasn't it? It had nothing to do with the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is supposed not to speak aloud. He should refrain from doing that. No loud speaking, Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you remember the question, Mr. Skrba?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've lost it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In that case I'll repeat it. The question was about Lukavac 93. But let me withdraw the question. We'll get to that later. Let me just put it to you right now that is it not the fact that the VRS considered that it had Sarajevo encircled and under blockade, and in fact they constantly emphasized the need to maintain that, so quite the contrary of being encircled by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were 70 per cent encircled, and I can say only a couple of sentences about this. This was the deployment and demarcation line after Lukavac 93, because we had no linkage with the Herzegovina Corps until 1993 and the Lukavac 93 operation. We used to be physically separated, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and the Herzegovina Corps. We had no point of contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. So two questions, again: Lukavac 93 had to do with the Herzegovina Corps and not the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably a part of the units of the Drina Corps participated with their assets and equipment and personnel in order to carry out that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I should have been clearer in my question. For the purposes of Lukavac 93, the SRK and the Drina Corps had already been linked, so the objective of Lukavac 93 was linking the SRK and the Herzegovina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Drina Corps was not able to link up with the Herzegovina Corps. First of all, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps would have to link up with the Herzegovina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so it was linking your corps with the Herzegovina Corps, whereas your corps was already linked to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Leaning on the right-hand side on the Herzegovina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, I want to go back to something you just told us. Yesterday in court and in your statement you are talking about this double encirclement. Now, you're just telling us that, in fact, it was a 70 per cent encircled; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, the Sarajevo Corps did not have any access towards south and south-east because that territory was held by Muslim forces that were linking up with Gorazde. So we had no physical linkage with the Herzegovina Corps. And our right-hand neighbour, the Drina Corps, had Muslim forces up to Nisici, so there was an external ring around them by the Muslim forces all the way around Sarajevo north and south-east, again towards Mount Jahorina and Gorazde. It was almost a full circle. There was just a little opening, 25 per cent of the territory behind the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, let's go to a few documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Can we please have P1963.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: While we're waiting for this document, Mr. Skrba, I'll tell you it is a directive for further operations from General Mladic dated August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And if we could please go to page English 3 and B/C/S 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, under the section headed: "Operation Objectives," we see, and I'll read: "Prevent the breaking of the blockade of Sarajevo." And then a few lines down: "Keep Sarajevo firmly under blockade and prevent its breaking." And perhaps that last word would be better translated as "break through." I believe in B/C/S it is the word "deblokadu." Mr. Skrba, it's clear from this document that Sarajevo was under blockade by the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I see. So your position, your interpretation of this document continues to be that it was the ABiH that was blockading the SRK; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We'll go to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Can I please have 65 ter 11410.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And while we're waiting -- I think we have that up. This is an SRK command order to all corps, and it's -- I believe it's type signed by Tomislav Sipcic, dated 8 August 1992. If we could please have page English 2 and B/C/S 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if I could just have a moment to find the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Under -- if I could direct your attention, Mr. Skrba, to the paragraph under the words -- the words "I have decided," do you see where it says: "The following tasks: To prevent the breaking of the blocked of Sarajevo and by taking appropriate actions simultaneously prevent fuelling of the Ustasha forces," and so on. But you see there the reference to the breaking of the blockade of Sarajevo, to prevent that; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Is it still your position that this is not true, that Sarajevo was not under blockade? This is from your corps.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's written here, but factually, the forces of the ABH always had open space through Butmir, and they used this passage mainly by night. And later on, after digging the tunnel, they had free passage, and hundreds of thousands of people passed through. They delivered food and power and supplies, so I cannot believe in the story of the blockade when I know that my own neighbours had to pay amounts like 5.000, 10.000 Deutschmarks to get out through that tunnel. Even the Muslims had to pay. They called it later the tunnel of salvation. In my area of responsibility, I never once fired at those people when they were getting out across the runway, wherever I could see them, because I considered them as civilians and I shouldn't shoot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you the following: You are saying there was no blockade because people at night or through the tunnel went in westerly direction. Now, the fact that some people escape doesn't mean that there is no blockade. It would be like saying in a prison you are free to go because people escape from prisons. That would not make a prison any less a prison, isn't it? Mr. Mladic, you are supposed to remain seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to mention one fact that we saw on the television in the federation when they held press conferences and the -- Delic, who was commander then, would say: "I'm going to Mount Igman this afternoon." How could he go if he didn't have a free passage? So those who wanted to leave could leave. Various delegations travelling abroad out of Sarajevo, they would use these passages for free such as the tunnel, but poorer people had to pay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it is your position that since people managed to get out, sometimes paying a heavy price for it, that means that there was no blockade and that all the military documents, as we see them on the screen, are for that reason wrong and there was no blockade nor was there a blockade intended. Is that how we have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was not 100 per cent. Because even if you look at their own TV programmes, they celebrate August 1993, the opening of the tunnel, and they always had communications for people and for equipment and for power supplies, and in the end even their military units passed by night to other areas outside of Sarajevo to fight because that was the shortest way, 1.200 metres, and the whole sector was under the control of UNPROFOR, which controlled the airport and made sure that UNPROFOR delegations and air-lifts can land safely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Carefully listening to your answers, it seems that you're explaining to us that the encirclement or a blockade was not fully effective for the 100 per cent because people managed to escape. Is that well understood and that for that reason you consider it not to have been a blockade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's about people who -- I was talking about people who wanted to get out. But I was talking about their military. They could have personnel coming in and out of the city whenever they liked, and that was possible across the runway or through the tunnel. And, of course, there was a security perimeter around so that, you know, the military could not get out -- outside of the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, I'm also looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm wondering if perhaps I could, because we're running out of time, otherwise just tender this document and leave that until tomorrow -- I'm sorry, rather than leave it until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You tender it now. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 11410 receives number P6522, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. We'll adjourn for the day and we'll resume -- but not until after -- I mean, we'll not adjourn until after the witness has left the courtroom. Would you please -- because I first want to instruct you -- yes, one second. I first want to instruct you that, as I instructed you yesterday, that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that was testimony given already or still to be given tomorrow. If that is clear to you, we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope we'll finish so I can go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a fair chance we will. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 22nd of May, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 22nd day of May, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.21 p.m.,
